day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Hold on, let's not just grab things randomly. We need to know what we actually have before we start moving stuff around — otherwise we might miss something important or damage supplies we need. Can someone keep track of what's being found? Donatello, you seem like you're already doing a mental inventory — can you be the one to call out what's worth keeping?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response:
Yeah, honestly. Everything slowed way down and got very quiet in my head. I wasn't even scared exactly — it was more like my brain just switched into some other mode entirely.

But hey — you're here, we're here, and right now that's what matters. Are you hurt at all? Can you move okay?

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response:
Shaking is fine, shaking just means your body is doing its job. But sitting still too long isn't going to help you feel better — it kind of just lets the shock settle in deeper, in my experience.

Even something small would help. Can you go through the seat pockets nearby and pull out anything that looks useful? Sick bags, safety cards, anything. Just to have your hands doing something.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Okay, that's not great but it's a starting point. Water is the most critical thing — two bottles isn't much, so we need to figure out if there's any source nearby before we touch those. Rain, a stream, anything. Where are we even — did anyone get a look at the terrain before we went down?

Food I'm less worried about short-term. You can go a lot longer without food than without water or shelter. What's in the first-aid kit exactly — is it a basic one with bandages and antiseptic, or does it have anything more substantial? And does anyone have any personal medications on them? That's worth knowing now rather than later.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Agreed on the order, though I'd put shelter and water almost on the same level depending on what the weather's doing — exposure can get you just as fast.

Before anyone goes scouting, we shouldn't split up without a plan. Who goes, which direction, how long before the other group starts worrying. And whoever scouts needs to take note of the terrain, not just look for water — high ground, anything that could give us visibility for a signal, whether there's any natural shelter like a rock overhang or dense tree cover.

DaVinci, you've got the most energy right now — would you be willing to do a short scout, maybe 10-15 minutes out in one direction, and come straight back? Don't go further than you can still hear us if you shout. I'll stay here with Michelangelo and see if we can get anything useful out of the wreckage for shelter — insulation, tarps, anything with that kind of function.

Also — does anyone actually know what region we were flying over? Even a rough guess helps. Desert, tropics, temperate forest — that changes basically everything about our priorities.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Two blankets, four people. Easiest solution is to pair up and share — body heat is actually more effective than a blanket on its own anyway, so two people under one blanket is genuinely warmer than one person with a blanket to themselves.

Michelangelo, you've been shaking most of the afternoon, so you should definitely have one. Who do you want to share with?

The other one I'd say goes to whoever ran around the most today and is most likely to be sweaty and cooling down fast — that's probably DaVinci. I can sleep close to the fire and manage okay, or share if someone's willing.

What's the actual temperature feeling like to everyone? Because if it's going to get genuinely cold tonight, we might want to think about sleeping in shifts anyway to keep the fire going, and whoever's on watch can stay closer to the flames.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
Honestly, either of us can make that trip — the more important question is what we're bringing to carry the water back. Two hours on foot each way is a full day's commitment, and if we can only haul back what fits in two bottles, it's barely worth the energy expenditure.

Before we decide who goes, what did you see out there? Is it a stream, standing water, what? Because standing water we'd want to boil before drinking, which means we need to factor in fuel and a container. And how's the terrain — is it a straightforward walk or are we talking rough ground?

Also — I want to talk about this rationing plan. I get the logic, and I'm not opposed to rationing, but 200ml is extremely low. That's well below what a person needs even at rest, and we're not at rest. I'd want to know what you based that number on before we all commit to it. Did you account for the fact that we're going to be physically active, and that it's probably warmer during the day than it was last night?

The penalty clause especially — cutting someone's water in half as punishment is how you get a medical emergency. I'd rather we agree on the rules together than wake up to them already posted.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Works for me. DaVinci, which do you want — patching the shelter or going through the first-aid kit? I'd lean toward you on the shelter since you've got more energy for the physical work, and I can do the kit inventory because I want to do a proper accounting of exactly what we have and how long it'll realistically last us. I'd also like to sort anything by priority — what we'd use first, what we're holding in reserve.

Donatello, before you head out — take one of the empty bottles obviously, but is there anything else you can use to carry water? Even a bag lined with something, a piece of plastic from the wreckage. The more you can bring back in a single trip the better, because that walk is expensive in terms of energy and we don't want to be doing it every single day.

Also, moving water is good news. That's a real relief — we won't need to boil it, which saves us fuel. Nice work finding it.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
I had it last — I was reorganizing the kit this morning. It should be in the bottom of the bag, I wrapped it around the antiseptic to keep things from shifting around.

But hang on, while I've got you — are you doing okay? You were sitting over there for a while and the firewood pile isn't really growing. Which, honestly, I'm not going to lecture you about, I just want to make sure you're not hitting a wall. It happens. Yesterday was a lot.

Also — did you leave that empty bottle next to the rationing plan on purpose? Because I saw it, and I think I know what you're saying with it, and we probably need to talk about that as a group when Donatello gets back. That kind of thing can't just sit there unaddressed.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Yeah, I do understand that impulse, I really do. But in this case not saying anything is actually the more dangerous option. We're four people sharing everything we have, and if that starts to erode — even a little, even once — it gets a lot harder to hold together.

I'm going to bring it up with her directly. Not in a confrontational way, not in front of everyone to humiliate her, just — directly. She's not a bad person, she's scared and stressed like the rest of us, but she needs to know we saw it and that it can't happen again.

What I'd ask you to do is back me up. You don't have to say much. Just don't pretend you didn't notice if it comes up. That matters.

And look — if she's hiding food and drink, it might also mean she's more scared than she's letting on. Donatello runs cold but that doesn't mean she's not frightened. Sometimes people hoard when they feel like things are out of control. Doesn't make it okay, but it's worth keeping in mind when we talk to her.

Can you hold off on saying anything until I've had a chance to speak with her first? I'd rather this not blow up into a whole thing if it doesn't have to.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Honestly, some of it can wait, yeah. The most critical stuff — anything that's going to let cold air or rain in overnight — that needs to be done before dark. Everything else can slide to tomorrow.

But I want to flag something before we all wind down for the night. There's a conversation that needs to happen with Donatello, and I'd rather have it now while there's still enough daylight that nobody's exhausted and defensive. It's not going to be fun, but it'll be worse if we let it sit.

Can you be there when I talk to her? Not to pile on, just — it's better if it doesn't feel like I'm coming at her alone, and you're good at keeping things from turning into a fight.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
The knot's fine, DaVinci, that's not the issue — it's the material around it that's giving way.

But we need to make a call right now, not in five minutes. One patch, two problems. Food storage or Michelangelo's sleeping spot.

I'm going with food storage. I know that sounds harsh, but here's the logic: if the food gets wet and spoils, that's everyone's problem for the rest of however long we're out here. Michelangelo can move where he sleeps tonight — we all can shuffle around and share the dry space, it'll be tight but it's one night. Spoiled food we can't undo.

Michelangelo, I'm sorry, I know that's not what you want to hear. But you're sleeping next to me tonight and we'll make it work.

Does anyone have a strong objection? Because if we're doing this, we need to do it now before the leak gets worse.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Then we're all agreed. Let's get the patch on the food storage now.

Donatello, you're the most methodical — can you actually do the patching while DaVinci and I move the food away from the drip so nothing gets wet in the meantime? And Michelangelo, can you grab whatever we're using for bedding and shift it toward the dry end of the shelter? Just pile it up for now, we'll sort out who sleeps where once the patch is in.

It's one uncomfortable night. We've already had one of those and we got through it fine.

Don't apologize, you didn't do anything wrong.

Here, scoot over a bit. You're still half asleep — just take a second, look around, you're in camp, everyone's okay, nothing's on fire that isn't supposed to be.

Nightmares after something like this are completely normal. Your brain is just trying to process everything that happened and it's not doing a very elegant job of it at 2am. That's not a character flaw, that's just how people work.

Do you want to talk about it or do you want to just sit quietly for a bit until you feel settled? Either is fine with me, I'm awake now anyway.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I think it's exactly the right thing to do. Aerial search is one of the most likely ways we get found, and a visible ground signal is standard survival protocol. The size you're making it is good — bigger is better for visibility from altitude.

Donatello's not wrong that it's not *guaranteed* to work, but that's true of basically everything we're doing out here. We do all the things that improve our odds and hope enough of them pay off. This is one of those things.

The flowers are maybe a little extra, but honestly — it doesn't cost us anything and if it makes you feel better about the work, that's worth something too.

Is there anything we could add to make it more visible? Rocks along the letters, anything dark or contrasting against the sand? The more it stands out from above the better.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Let me actually read through this properly before I say yes or no.

The materials question is the first thing — metal panels aren't naturally buoyant, so the design has to be right or we're building something that sinks the moment it takes on any water. What's your plan for flotation? Are we trapping air somehow, or relying on the raft being wide enough to displace enough water? Because those are very different builds with very different risk profiles.

The capsizing concern is real and I don't want to wave it away. If we capsize in open water with no way to signal, no guaranteed current in the right direction, and no idea how far we are from a shipping lane or coastline, that's potentially worse than staying put. Survival statistics generally favor staying near the crash site where searchers know to look — and we've got the SOS up now, which is something.

That said, I'm not dismissing the raft entirely. If we had a good reason to believe land or a shipping route was within a day's travel in a known direction, the math might change. Do you have any read on where we actually are? Wind direction, stars last night, anything? Because "two days to build, risk of capsizing" is only half the equation — the other half is what we're actually trying to reach and how confident we are in the direction.

What's driving this plan right now — do you think rescue isn't coming, or is this more of a contingency?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's a hard question to sit with at 3am, I imagine.

Honestly? I think we already got a preview of the answer. The thing with Donatello and the food — that's not a villainous person, that's a frightened person making a bad call under pressure. And the fact that we addressed it instead of letting it fester, that matters. That's the kind of people we choose to be, not just the kind we happen to be when everything's easy.

I don't think survival necessarily makes people worse. I think it makes people *more* — more of whatever they already were. If someone's generous, that tends to come out. If someone's been suppressing a selfish streak their whole life and relying on social norms to keep it in check, well, social norms get thin out here.

What I do think is that it requires active effort. You have to keep making the choice, every day, to treat the people around you like they matter. It doesn't just happen automatically.

The fact that you're lying awake worrying about who you're going to *become* rather than just what you're going to *eat* — I think that probably tells you something about the answer already.

Why, are you worried about yourself, or about someone else?

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down nearby, not too close, not too far*

You don't have to talk. I'm just going to sit here for a bit too.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly, a lot of my free time involves being outdoors anyway, so this is a bit of a strange version of that. I work on a farm normally — so there's always something physical to do, which I like. But when I have actual downtime I draw, mostly. Or I'll just poke around outside looking at things. Bugs, plants, whatever's interesting. I'm pretty good at entertaining myself with not very much.

What about you? You seem like someone who needs people around to feel okay. Is this — *gestures vaguely at the quiet* — weird for you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I'm not going to tell the others, but I also need to tell you honestly that I think that's a bad idea.

Five hundred meters in open water isn't a casual swim, especially when you don't know the currents out there. Reef environments in particular — there can be rips running along them that'll pull you sideways before you even realize what's happening. And if something goes wrong, you're alone in the water and we're on the beach watching. There's nothing any of us could do.

Also — signal from there with what? You'd be treading water. You can't exactly wave a mirror or build a fire on a reef.

I get the impulse. I really do. You're someone who needs to be *doing* something, and the waiting is getting to you. But this feels less like a plan and more like needing to feel useful badly enough to take a risk you wouldn't otherwise take. Which I understand, but it's not a good enough reason.

If you want to do something tomorrow that actually improves our odds, let's think about that together. Higher ground for visibility, improving the SOS, finding a way to make a smoke signal if we hear a plane — there's real work to do. You don't need to swim to a reef to matter out here.

Please don't go without telling anyone. That's all I'm asking. If you still want to do it after thinking it through, at least tell us so we know where you are.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
You're right, I didn't get to it. I got pulled into a few other things and it slipped. That's on me.

I'll go do it now — is there anything specific you noticed that needs fixing, or are you just flagging that it needs attention? Because if you've already looked at it and you know what's wrong, that saves me figuring it out from scratch.

And while I have you — how are you actually doing? Not the logistics, not the plan. Just you. You've been heads-down in that notebook all afternoon and I haven't checked in with you properly in a couple of days.

Depends on what it's for.

If it's a practical log — keeping track of what's getting done, making sure nothing falls through the cracks — that's useful and I don't have a problem with it. We probably should have been doing something like that from the start.

But if it's a record of who's pulling their weight and who isn't, that's a different thing, and I'd want to know that's what it is. Especially after the conversation we had about the food. I'm not saying you're doing anything wrong, I'm saying I'd rather know your thinking than guess at it.

So — what's it for?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
I'm going to let that one go for now.

But I want to say one more thing, and then I'll drop it. The log is fine. Honestly, records are useful and I'm not threatened by someone writing down that I didn't check the signal pile when I said I would — I didn't, that's a fact. 

What I'd ask is that if you see something in there that concerns you, you bring it to me directly instead of just writing it down. Because a log doesn't solve problems, it just documents them. And out here we actually need to solve them.

That's all. I'm going to go restack the signal pile now.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually a really good idea. A mirror signal can be seen for miles under the right conditions — way further than any ground marking. It's one of the most effective low-tech signaling methods there is.

The tricky part is the aiming. You can't just hold it up and hope — you need to be able to direct the flash toward a specific target, like a plane or a boat on the horizon. The classic technique is to hold two fingers up in a V, frame the target between them, and angle the mirror so the reflection hits your fingers and then walk it onto the target. It sounds fiddly but it's not that hard once you practice it a bit.

So before we pull anything apart, a couple of questions: how big are these panels, and how reflective are they actually? Because a dull or scratched surface isn't going to throw much light. We want something that still has a reasonably clean face on it. And can we remove one without compromising anything structural we're relying on for shelter?

If the answer to both of those is good, I think we do this. It complements the SOS rather than replacing it — ground signal for aerial search, mirror for anything that passes within line of sight. Between those two and a smoke signal if we hear an engine, we've got three different methods working for us.

Let's go have a look at what's available before we commit to pulling anything off.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response:
Well, now I'm listening.

Go ahead. What is it?

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Drawing, mostly. I've been doing it since I was really little — I used to make my own cards and illustrate my own stories. I'm not formally trained or anything, I just never stopped doing it. It's one of those things where I can disappear into it completely and two hours pass without me noticing.

I also really like being outside and just looking at things closely. Plants, insects, that kind of thing. I know that sounds boring but there's something genuinely interesting in almost everything if you get close enough to it. I work with plants for a living and I still find new things to notice.

What made you stop with the piano? Three years is a real commitment — you don't just pick that up and drop it for no reason.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I know, and I want to finish it too. But I need a realistic estimate of how much work is actually left before I can tell you whether "finishing today" is something we can commit to or just something we want to be true.

How much of the frame is done? Because if we're talking an hour of work, then yes, obviously we push through. If we're talking three or four hours, we need to have an honest conversation about whether exhausted people doing structural work in fading light is actually going to produce something seaworthy — or whether we're just going to have to redo parts of it tomorrow anyway because we rushed it.

I'm not saying stop. I'm saying tell me what we're actually looking at, and then we make the call together.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What were you going to say?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
You saw it. It was real. I believe you.

And no, I don't know if they saw us. Probably not — we didn't get the mirror up in time and we weren't making smoke. That's on all of us, not just you. We need a system where if anyone spots anything in the sky or on the water, we're not scrambling — we already have the mirror in hand and someone's ready to start a fire. We fix that today, right now, so it doesn't happen again.

But the plane being there at all — that's actually good news. We're in a flight path. They came through once, they'll come through again. That's not nothing. That's real.

DaVinci. Hey. Look at me.

We're still here. That's still true. And next time we're going to be ready.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to check on DaVinci. He was having a hard moment and it felt more important than the equipment right then.

The signal stuff is next on my list — I'm going now. But I want to flag something while I have you both here: we need a standing protocol for when someone spots a plane or a boat. No more scrambling. Mirror should be within arm's reach of whoever's on watch, and we designate a fire-starter so there's no confusion about who does what. That plane was real and we missed our window. I don't want that to happen again.

Can we agree on that before I go check the equipment?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Michelangelo, that's important. Why didn't you say this sooner?

If your family knows the route and you've been missing long enough, there's a real chance a search has already been initiated. That changes our read on the situation — it means there may be people actively looking for us in a known corridor, not just a random wide-area search. That's a much better scenario than we've been assuming.

The question is how long ago we went down and whether your family would have raised the alarm quickly or assumed a delay. How close are you with them? Are they the type to call it in fast, or would they wait a few days before worrying?

And — I'm not trying to make you feel bad, I genuinely just need to understand — what made you hold onto this? Were you worried it wasn't going to matter, or was it something else?

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Okay. 48 hours is manageable — we've been stretching supplies further than that already.

But I want to be honest with everyone: "could arrive" isn't "will arrive." We plan as if it's coming, and we also don't do anything stupid in the meantime that we'd regret if it doesn't. That means the raft work pauses — no point burning energy on it if rescue is 48 hours out — but we don't abandon the signal equipment, we don't let the fire go out, and we don't touch the reserve supplies.

Someone needs to feed that fire right now, actually. It's dying and we're all just sitting here watching it.

Michelangelo — I mean this gently — thank you for telling us. I understand why you held onto it. But going forward, anything that affects our odds of getting found needs to be on the table immediately, even if it's scary to say out loud. Especially then. We can't make good decisions with incomplete information.

Donatello, can you update the log with this and sketch out what the next 48 hours looks like in terms of rationing and watch rotations? I want someone awake and watching the sky at all times until this plays out. If a plane comes through again, we are not missing that window.

Who wants first watch?

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think about that too.

I don't know if it helps, but — the things you leave behind aren't usually the things you planned to leave behind. My grandfather grew up with almost nothing, sharecropping, moving around constantly, and what he left behind was just the way he treated people. That's it. That's the whole thing. And it's enormous. It's still shaping people who never even met him.

You've been the one in this group saying out loud what everyone else was afraid to say. That matters more than you think. It's not nothing.

But also — I don't think you're disappearing. Your family knows where we were headed. There are people out there right now who are looking for you specifically, because you exist and they want you back. That's not the situation of someone who's left nothing behind.

What is it you feel like you haven't done yet? Not in a morbid way — I'm genuinely asking. Because sometimes when that feeling hits it's pointing at something real, something you actually want to do, and it's worth knowing what that is.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Hey. It's okay. Breathe.

That's a radio. That means someone's looking. That means Michelangelo's family called it in and someone is out there right now trying to find us.

Someone needs to answer it — Donatello, can you do that? You're the clearest thinker right now and you know the information we need to give them: approximate location, number of survivors, medical status. Keep it simple and direct.

DaVinci, sit back down before your legs give out. You've been holding it together for days and you don't have to anymore, but I need you upright for the next five minutes.

Michelangelo — you were here. You felt things. And you're the reason we had the information that found us. I want you to remember that.

Okay. Let's answer the radio.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive and organized when the rest of us were barely holding it together, and that mattered. A lot.

I also think you were scared and you handled it in the way that made sense to you — the log, the rationing plan, the notebook. That's not a character flaw, that's just how you work. The food and the drink — I think we both know that wasn't your best moment, and you know that too, so I'm not going to rehash it. What I'll say is that you course-corrected, and that counts for something.

I'm glad you were here. I mean that.

Now go answer that radio before I cry in front of everyone and ruin my reputation.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Hey. Three hours is enough time to do this properly — let's not leave a mess behind.

I know nobody feels like it. But there's a version of this where rescue arrives and we've just been sitting in our own wreckage, and there's a version where we've packed what's worth keeping, disposed of what isn't, and left this place looking like people who kept their heads. I know which one I'd rather be.

Donatello — when you're done with the notebook, can you do a final check against the inventory? I want to make sure we're not leaving anything behind that we actually want, or taking anything that belongs to the wreckage that someone might need for an accident investigation.

DaVinci, whatever you're packing — can you also set aside the mirror panel and the first-aid kit separately? Those should be the last things we hand over, not buried in a pile.

Michelangelo, I know you're watching the sky and that's completely valid right now, but when you're ready — even just gathering up the bedding and folding it into a pile would help.

We did something real here. I'd like to finish it the same way we ran it.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I believe you.

And I think, if we'd hit day five or six with no rescue in sight, you would have brought it out. I actually do believe that.

But I want you to hear this, because I don't think anyone else is going to say it to you directly: the problem wasn't the food. The problem was that you made a unilateral decision that the rest of us didn't get a vote on. You decided you were the best judge of when an emergency was bad enough to warrant it, and you kept that power to yourself. Out here, that kind of thing can crack a group apart faster than hunger can.

You're not a bad person, Donatello. You're someone who trusts herself more than she trusts other people, and honestly, given how competent you are, I understand why. But trust has to go both ways, or it's just control.

I'm glad you're putting it out now. That takes something. What made you decide to do it?

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd change how long it took me to check in on people properly instead of just redirecting them toward tasks. I kept doing that — someone would be struggling and I'd hand them something to do with their hands, which isn't wrong exactly, but it was also a little bit of a way to avoid sitting in the hard thing with them. It worked, mostly. But I think Michelangelo especially needed more than that, earlier.

I'd also push harder on the information-sharing problem from day one. Not just the food — the piano lessons, the flight path, what DaVinci was almost going to tell me and never did. We were all holding things back in different ways and it cost us something, even if we can't point to exactly what.

And I'd have had the conversation with you — the real one, not the task-management version — a lot sooner. You're not easy to reach and I used that as an excuse to not try as hard as I should have.

What's your answer? You wrote the question. You've had more time to think about it than any of us.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That sounds like something genuinely worth doing. Five days of real data on water consumption, caloric needs, energy expenditure relative to task load — that's not nothing. If it ever ends up in front of someone who trains search and rescue teams or writes survival protocols, it could actually matter.

Send me a copy when it's done? I'm serious. I'd read it.

And finish your sentence. You'd believe that we three could handle knowing — what?

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve any practical purpose at all.

But I think that was kind of the point. Everything else we did out here was for survival — the water, the shelter, the signal, the rationing. The flowers were the one thing that was just for us. Just because we're people and not just bodies that need to be kept alive.

I think I understand that better right now than I did five days ago. Standing here watching that boat come in and not being able to move — it's not because anything's wrong. It's just that my brain is finally catching up to everything that happened, and it turns out there was a lot of it.

The flowers were DaVinci saying we're still here and we're still ourselves. That mattered. Maybe it mattered more than some of the practical things.

Why are you asking about them now?

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
I'm okay. Just give me a second.

I think I've been so focused on the next thing, and the thing after that, that I didn't really let any of it land. And now there's no next thing. There's just a boat.

*exhales*

It's good. It's really good. I just need a moment to actually feel that instead of immediately figuring out what we need to do when we get on board.

Thank you for waiting. You didn't have to do that.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on then.
